stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. live_data_statements: Results: Of 4,005 adolescents screened, 1465 met eligibility, 727 consented and 560 were enrolled.
Participants were 12-14 year-old pupils (School years 7-9) from 11 state-maintained secondary schools in London and the South East of England.
Participants were eligible if they had a Total Difficulties score of 15 or above on SDQ (Goodman et al., 1998).
Participants completed assessments independently on a tablet device to minimise the impact of the researcher presence on the outcome data collection.
Participants were screened for eligibility in the school term preceding their enrolment into the trial.
The participants are clustered in schools and year groups.
Participants were included in these analyses if they provided data for at least one time point.
Of those eligible, parental consent was received for 727 (49.63% of eligible pupils) and 560 participants were enrolled into the trial.
Figure 1: CONSORT Diagram demonstrating the number of participants enrolled in the trial and those retained until 1-year follow-up.
For the per-protocol analysis, 243 (86 %) of intervention participants were classed as adherent and included.

The trial also demonstrates the feasibility of a whole-school screening-to-intervention pathway: of 4,005 pupils screened, approximately 37% were identified as at-risk, 50% consented to take part and 560 were enrolled, with 90% retained at the 1-year follow-up.
Informed consent was obtained from all participants and their parents/carers prior to taking part in the study.

text.text: Background: Rates of mental health problems in adolescents have increased in the last decade, prompting urgent calls for effective, scalable preventative interventions.

To determine whether a novel, group-based, transdiagnostic indicated prevention programme (Building Resilience through Socioemotional Training; ReSET), delivered through existing school mental health provision, improves mental health and wellbeing in at-risk adolescents.

Methods: Two-arm cluster randomised controlled superiority trial (1:1) evaluating ReSET plus usual care versus usual care only, with outcomes assessed immediately post-intervention and at 12-month follow-up.

Adolescents aged 12-14 identified through whole-school screening as scoring in the top 25th percentile for overall psychopathology symptoms, in schools selected to over-represent high-need communities (≥30% free school meals eligibility).

ReSET is an 8session group -based intervention that targets two key mechanisms implicated in risk for psychopathology in adolescents -the quality and quantity of social relationships and emotional processing.
Pre-registered co-primary outcomes were overall self-reported psychopathology (SDQ) and wellbeing (WEMWBS), assessed immediately post-intervention and at 12-month follow-up.
Results: Of 4,005 adolescents screened, 1465 met eligibility, 727 consented and 560 were enrolled.
There was no evidence of intervention effects on either co-primary outcome immediately post-intervention.
At 12-month follow-up, there was evidence of improvement in overall psychopathology (adjusted mean difference -1.36, 97.5% CI -2.23 to -0.50, p=0.0004; SMD=0.25, 95% CI 0.11 to 0.42).

Secondary outcomes showed a consistent pattern: no effects immediately post-intervention, but significant benefits for anxiety, depression, general psychopathology, and internalising symptoms at 12-month follow-up.
No effects on externalising symptoms were observed at either timepoint.

The delayed emergence of benefit is consistent with a skills-based prevention model in which adolescents acquire skills that support resilient functioning when facing subsequent emotional and interpersonal challenges.

These findings suggest that transdiagnostic interventions targeting socioemotional processes have the potential to prevent common adolescent mental health problems, though replication and longer-term evaluation are needed.

In light of the rising rates of mental ill-health among adolescents, there have been urgent calls to increase the availability of scalable interventions that prevent the onset or worsening of mental health problems in this age group (McGorry et al., 2024).
text.formatted: In light of the rising rates of mental ill-health among adolescents, there have been urgent calls to increase the availability of scalable interventions that prevent the onset or worsening of mental health problems in this age group <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(McGorry et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: However, evidence suggests that universal prevention programmes have limited impact and in some cases may even lead to harm (Andrews et al., 2023).
text.formatted: However, evidence suggests that universal prevention programmes have limited impact and in some cases may even lead to harm <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Andrews et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Indicated prevention appears to be a more feasible approach (Andrews & Foulkes, 2025).
text.formatted: Indicated prevention appears to be a more feasible approach <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Andrews & Foulkes, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Further, most existing indicated prevention programmes target specific conditions (most commonly depression), limiting their utility for addressing the broader mental health needs of adolescent populations.

Longitudinal studies show that adolescents may experience multiple overlapping mental health difficulties and may transition between diagnoses over time, making disorder-specific targeting potentially challenging (Dalgleish et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Longitudinal studies show that adolescents may experience multiple overlapping mental health difficulties and may transition between diagnoses over time, making disorder-specific targeting potentially challenging <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Dalgleish et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: A transdiagnostic approach provides a logical strategy to address this challenge by targeting common mechanisms that operate across disorders, or, alternatively, by providing flexible therapies that address multiple problem areas (Astle et al., 2024; Dalgleish et al., 2020; McGorry et al., 2018).
text.formatted: A transdiagnostic approach provides a logical strategy to address this challenge by targeting common mechanisms that operate across disorders, or, alternatively, by providing flexible therapies that address multiple problem areas <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Astle et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Dalgleish et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">McGorry et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: In a recent systematic review, Du Toit et al. (2025) identified only one full-scale trial of a transdiagnostic indicated prevention programme for adolescents. Jeppesen et al. (2021) tested the efficacy of a modular CBT programme for help-seeking adolescents aged 6-16 years scoring over the 90 th percentile for mental health problems.

(2025)</ref> identified only one full-scale trial of a transdiagnostic indicated prevention programme for adolescents. <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Jeppesen et al. (2021)</ref> tested the efficacy of a modular CBT programme for help-seeking adolescents aged 6-16 years scoring over the 90 th percentile for mental health problems.

text.text: The modular programme allowed therapists to select different treatment elements to match a young person's profile of presenting symptoms across different diagnostic domains.
Delivered by trained psychologists over 9-13 one-to-one sessions, the trial showed robust benefits for overall symptomatology at 3 and 6-month follow-ups.

This modular approach to transdiagnostic intervention, though promising, has some limitations, particularly the requirement that clear symptom profiles are already present, treatment sessions have to be one-to-one and skilled clinicians are required for delivery.
Given the level of need in the population, evaluating alternative approaches remains a priority, particularly those that can be brought to scale.
Here we report results from the ReSET trial, the first large-scale, adequately powered RCT of an indicated prevention programme targeting transdiagnostic mechanisms in youth psychopathology.

We adopted a whole-school screening approach to identify at-risk adolescents and bypass the help-seeking and referral barriers that typically prevent young people from accessing support, targeting those scoring in the top 25% of overall mental health symptoms.

This novel, group-based, intervention, Building Resilience through Socioemotional Training (ReSET) teaches skills targeting two mechanisms of change: communication skills and emotion processing abilities (Mitic et al., 2021).
text.formatted: This novel, group-based, intervention, Building Resilience through Socioemotional Training (ReSET) teaches skills targeting two mechanisms of change: communication skills and emotion processing abilities <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Mitic et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: The intervention exploits the dynamic relationship between young people's social interactions and their emotional functioning.

By equipping young people with the skills to manage their emotions and relationships more effectively, ReSET aims to disrupt the negative reciprocal cycles of emotional dysregulation and social difficulties that can drive the transition from sub-threshold symptoms to clinical disorder.
The intervention was designed to be delivered in schools using their existing mental health provision, to shorten the pathway from efficacy trial to implementation.

To address the targeted transdiagnostic mechanisms, ReSET integrated techniques from two distinct disciplinary backgrounds, clinical psychology/psychiatry and cognitive neuroscience (Lloyd, Law, et al., 2024; Viding et al., 2024).
text.formatted: To address the targeted transdiagnostic mechanisms, ReSET integrated techniques from two distinct disciplinary backgrounds, clinical psychology/psychiatry and cognitive neuroscience <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Lloyd, Law, et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Viding et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: To strengthen skills related to adolescents' communication abilities, ReSET adapted techniques used in Interpersonal Psychotherapy-Adolescent Skills Training (IPT-AST; Young et al., 2012).
text.formatted: To strengthen skills related to adolescents' communication abilities, ReSET adapted techniques used in Interpersonal Psychotherapy-Adolescent Skills Training (IPT-AST; <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Young et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: These adapted techniques were designed to support young people's relationships by teaching them social and communication skills that foster positive interactions and practising these skills through roleplay exercises.
When developing ReSET, specific content was also included to explain the important connection between relationships and emotions.

This content was designed to link the relationship focused work with the emotion processing skills trained via established computerised cognitive-emotional training tasks (Penton-Voak et al., 2013; Zsigo et al., 2024).
text.formatted: This content was designed to link the relationship focused work with the emotion processing skills trained via established computerised cognitive-emotional training tasks <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Penton-Voak et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Zsigo et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: The first of these encouraged young people to practice positive emotion regulation strategies (namely, distancing and reinterpretation) in response to fictional examples.
The second, the Interpretation Bias Training Task, modified young people's perceptions to view neutral/ambiguous faces as friendly rather than hostile.
ReSET thus focused on highlighting the reciprocal relation between social interactions and emotions (Lloyd, Law, et al., 2024) and their joint contribution to emotional health and wellbeing.

text.text: To ensure the novel intervention was acceptable to young people, ReSET underwent an extensive, co-produced development process, including pilot and feasibility testing (Lloyd et al., 2025; Lloyd, Law, et al., 2024; Lloyd, Wu, et al., 2024).

text.text: The trial also included an integrated process evaluation, exploring the experience of the young people who took part in the ReSET intervention (Lucas et al., 2026).

text.text: Because ReSET is a skills-based prevention programme, benefits were expected to consolidate as adolescents encounter subsequent emotional and interpersonal challenges; primary outcomes were therefore also assessed at 12-month follow-up.

The primary hypothesis was that among adolescents with increased risk of mental health, those who received the ReSET programme will have better mental health and well-being outcomes than those in the non-intervention arm.
The trial was registered on the ISRCTN registry on 20/04/2024 (ISRCTN88585916; see https://www.isrctn.com/ISRCTN88585916).

text.text: We conducted a parallel, cluster randomised controlled, multicentre superiority trial of the ReSET programme versus pupils' school provision as usual.
Outcome assessors were masked to allocation.
Owing to the nature of the intervention, participants and intervention providers could not be masked.
The trial took place in mainstream secondary schools in the Southeast of England, with a total of 11 participating schools across 12 study sites.
Pupil screening and informed consent were obtained via physical forms or the REDcap platform.
Parents and carers were provided with opt-out forms for the screening questionnaire.
Active consent was required from parents/carers and adolescents participating in the intervention and control arms of the trial.
Outcome measures were collected via the PsyTools platform.
The study received ethical approval from UCL's research ethics committee (ref: 21815/001).
For the study protocol, see (Viding et al., 2024).

text.text: Participants were 12-14 year-old pupils (School years 7-9) from 11 state-maintained secondary schools in London and the South East of England.
Participants were eligible if they had a Total Difficulties score of 15 or above on SDQ (Goodman et al., 1998).

text.text: This threshold was selected as it represented the top 25% of scores for adolescents of this age group, based on a nationally representative sample in the UK (University of Essex, 2022).

text.text: Pupils could be excluded from the trial if school staff identified them as having high rates of school absence or if they were not considered suitable for a group-based intervention, though this rarely occurred.
There were no other exclusion criteria and diagnoses of neurodivergence were recorded.
To encourage socioeconomic diversity in the sample, at least 30% of pupils at participating schools had to qualify for free school meals.
The primary endpoint for this trial was the assessment conducted immediately postintervention.

This decision reflected a cautious and pragmatic design choice, balancing statistical power and feasibility against the uncertainty inherent in longer-term follow-up in school-based trials, including potential attrition and school transitions.

Further, previous indicated prevention trials of closely related interventions, particularly IPT-AST, have reported detectable short-term improvements in mental health outcomes, making it reasonable to anticipate measurable post-intervention effects.

At the same time, the intervention was explicitly designed as a preventative, skillsbased programme, with the expectation that any benefits might consolidate over time as adolescents encountered new social and emotional challenges and enter a period of increased risk.
For this reason, outcomes were also assessed at 12 months from baseline as a key followup timepoint for evaluating potential preventative effects.
Randomisation was at the school year-group level with 1:1 randomisation.
Within schools, one year group was allocated to the intervention arm and the other to the control arm.
Randomisation was balanced across schools using block randomisation, implemented by an independent statistician (see Viding et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Randomisation was balanced across schools using block randomisation, implemented by an independent statistician (see <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Viding et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Only the independent statistician and project coordinator were aware of the randomisation schedule.
Neither the trial statistician nor assessors were aware of the randomisation schedule.
Participants completed assessments independently on a tablet device to minimise the impact of the researcher presence on the outcome data collection.
Where researchers were unblinded to the allocation, this was recorded along with the timepoint at which they were unblinded.
Participants were screened for eligibility in the school term preceding their enrolment into the trial.
Assessments of primary and secondary outcomes took place at the beginning of each school term (baseline), which were followed by the 8-week intervention for those in the intervention arm.
The primary endpoint assessment typically occurred at the end of that same term.
Follow-up data were collected for all primary and secondary outcomes 12 months after baseline.
The trial ran across several school terms, with 10 participants allocated to the intervention arm and 10 allocated to the control arm in any one school term.
ReSET is an 8-week group-based programme.

Beginning with a 1:1 meeting, participants then completed eight, 90-minute group-based sessions comprised of up to 10 adolescents, which involved a combination of discussion activities, role-plays, and app-based cognitive-emotional training.
Mid-way through the programme (weeks four or five), another 1:1 meeting is held to identify barriers to participation, monitor progress, and review key strategies.
Parents and/or carers are also invited to attend this mid-group meeting.
For further description of the intervention, see Supplementary Materials and Lloyd et al. (2025).

text.text: Facilitators delivering the intervention were pairs of trained mental health practitioners, including school staff trained in mental health support, Mental Health Support Teams from the charity sector or NHS, and members of the research team.
All facilitators completed two days of training prior to delivering the intervention.
The training was provided by a consultant clinical psychologist with extensive experience of IPT-AST and research team members with expertise of the cognitive-emotional training protocols.
During delivery of the intervention, facilitators had weekly supervision meetings with the consultant clinical psychologist who was the project clinical lead.
Fidelity checks were also completed by a member of the research team, who was not involved in delivering the intervention, in weeks one, two and five.
If areas of the intervention were not being delivered as intended, feedback and support was provided through weekly supervision meetings

The co-primary outcomes for this trial were overall psychopathology, measured using the total difficulties score on the SDQ (Goodman et al., 2000), and overall wellbeing (WEMWBS; Tennant et al., 2007).

Mental health secondary outcomes, closely aligned with the intervention's theoretical targets, assessed depression (Patient Health Questionnaire-8; PHQ-8; Kroenke et al., 2009)), and generalised anxiety (Generalised Anxiety Disorder Assessment-7; GAD-7; Spitzer et al., 2006).

Any adverse events reported in the intervention and control arms were recorded.
Adverse events were defined as incidents that required referral to a Child and Young Person Mental Health Support Team, Child and Adolescent Mental Health Service (CAMHS), GP, or emergency services.

The participants are clustered in schools and year groups.
Participants in the intervention arm are additionally clustered in ReSET groups in the intervention arm, but there is no such additional clustering in the control arm.
The prespecified primary outcome analysis was therefore a partially clustered linear mixed effects model with normally distributed heteroscedastic errors (Candlish et al., 2018).

text.text: This model includes a random effect for intervention groups, to account for partial clustering.

It also controls for clustering within schools via a random effect and for the school year (or cohort), the timing of the measurement (i.e. school term), and baseline outcome measure score via fixed effects.
These complex models turned out to be difficult to fit and failed to converge for most outcomes.
Where this was the case, we followed the procedure prespecified for this eventuality in the SAP, and fitted the most complex model possible.
For the two primary outcomes, this was a mixed effects linear regression with a random intercept for school, but not for ReSET groups.

There were 14 adverse events, each occurring with unique individuals in the intervention arm.

These events were deemed to be unrelated to the trial, as they involved safeguarding disclosures pertaining to events that had occurred prior to enrolment and were disclosed through contact with a ReSET facilitator.
For the per-protocol analysis, 243 (86 %) of intervention participants were classed as adherent and included.

Effect estimates and confidence intervals from the per-protocol analysis were similar to those from the intent-to-treat analysis reported, and in no case would have led to substantively different conclusions.
The same was true for all sensitivity analyses (see Supplementary Materials Sections 5-8).

Further, we found no evidence of differences between the trial arms in an analysis of treatment received after the intervention (which due to resource constraints in the schools was collected in a single 'census' of current provision after all the intervention groups had ended across all schools; see Supplementary Materials).

We estimated that when applied at a population level the intervention would avert approximately 1,727 cases per 100,000 adolescents in this age group and timeframe, representing approximately 19% of the pre-intervention case burden, assuming a normal distribution with mean 9 and SD 6, targeting of the top 25% on SDQ total scores, an effect size of d = .25 (the 1-year follow-up effect on the mental health primary outcome), uptake of 50% (the rate achieved in this study), and a clinical threshold of 17 on the SDQ total score.
This approach of course assumes that only adolescents scoring at or above the clinical threshold benefit from the intervention, which is unlikely to be true in practice.

This cluster-randomised controlled trial is the first to evaluate an indicated prevention programme for adolescents targeting skills relevant for transdiagnostic mechanisms, designed to be scalable by being delivered in groups, and embedded in schools' existing mental health provision.
At the primary endpoint, immediately post-intervention, we found no evidence of benefit on either overall psychopathology or wellbeing.

In contrast, at 12-month follow-up, adolescents allocated to the intervention arm showed statistically robust reductions in overall psychopathology and internalising symptoms, relative to those receiving usual school provision.
Effect sizes were consistent across multiple related outcomes.

Sensitivity analyses suggested the results were robust to variations in adherence (though session attendance was generally high), and patterns of missing data (which was generally low, even at 12-month follow-up).

There was little evidence of differences in patterns of referral or service use between the two arms of the trial during or after the intervention that might otherwise explain the long-term benefits we observed.
The findings suggest that the trial's primary evaluation endpoint happened too early to capture the gradual impact of this skills-focused indicated prevention programme.

In hindsight, the apparent delayed impact may not be surprising, as ReSET was not designed to target symptoms directly; rather, the programme was designed to upskill young people to manage their emotions and social interactions more effectively.

Benefits to mental health symptoms from this type of intervention are likely to accrue gradually, as young people apply their newly acquired skills to the emotional or social challenges they currently face and to new challenges they encounter over time.

The pattern of findings is similar to that reported by Clarke et al (1995), which found no benefits of a CBT-based indicated prevention programme for depression in adolescents immediately post-intervention but consistent benefits 12 and 24 months later.

text.text: We selected the primary endpoint to be immediately post-intervention primarily to mitigate the risks to statistical power posed by potential attrition over time; however, the concern about attrition turned out to be unwarranted, as follow-up rates after a year were very high (~90%).
We recommend that future research includes evaluation immediately after, 3 months, 6 months and 12 months post-intervention, to track the evolution of its impact.

At 12-month follow-up, adolescents allocated to the intervention arm showed statistically robust reductions in overall psychopathology and internalising symptoms, relative to those receiving usual school provision.

Although effect sizes were modest, they were consistent across multiple related outcomes and marginally larger than those reported in other school-based mental health prevention trials with at least medium-term (6-months+) follow-up (Werner-Seidler et al., 2017).

text.text: One possible mechanism for this delayed benefit is that the intervening time between the intervention and 12-month follow-up is one in which adolescents face increasing emotional and interpersonal challenges.

These exposures may provide greater opportunity to deploy the skills acquired during the programme and experience their benefit, positively impacting mental health, but requiring time to show effects.
Indeed, this interpretation is consistent with literature on 'sleeper effects' of psychosocial interventions (Wade et al., 2022), which also show delayed benefit.

text.text: The bifactor model used to derive the latent factor scores yields orthogonal factors, meaning that the p-factor (general psychopathology) and the internalising and externalizing factors represent statistically independent dimensions of psychopathology.
The significant effects on the p-factor and internalizing factor at 1 year follow up therefore represent evidence of separate, independent benefits of the intervention.
The convergent findings for GAD-7 and PHQ-8 further corroborate this pattern across different measurement approaches.
The results therefore suggest that the programme produced benefits to both general distress, or global mental health difficulties, and to symptoms of depression and anxiety specifically.

Notably however, ReSET did not improve externalising symptoms at either follow-up, with effects favouring the control arm; mean differences between trial arms were small and confidence intervals wide and inclusive of zero at both timepoints.

The lack of impact on externalizing problems may reflect real limitations in the scope of impact of this intervention or, alternatively, might reflect limitations in the scope for identifying improvements due the symptom profiles of young people entering the trial and/or overlap between externalizing symptoms and the global p-factor scores.
It should also be noted that IPT-AST has typically been trialled for internalising symptoms (Young et al., 2012).
text.formatted: It should also be noted that IPT-AST has typically been trialled for internalising symptoms <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Young et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: As ReSET utilised features of IPT-AST in combination with cognitive-emotional training tasks, it may be that the intervention was not optimised to reduce externalising problems.

Nevertheless, in light of some indications in past literature that group-based interventions can be unhelpful for youth with conduct problems (Dishion et al., 1999), the lack of negative impacts on externalizing problems in this trial is noteworthy.

text.text: In this trial, secondary social network outcomes showed small to moderate differences favouring the control group at both follow-up timepoints.

These findings raise the possibility that participation in the intervention was associated with changes in peer networks, including fewer friendship nominations or a narrower set of peers identified as sources of advice.

However, it should be noted that the number of nominations does not indicate the quality of participants' relationships, which may be more important for mental health outcomes (Mitic et al., 2021) and differences tended to diminish at 1 year follow-up.

text.text: In addition, evidence from a process evaluation conducted in parallel with the trial suggested that young people developed new peer connections through taking part in the intervention, which were found to be helpful for managing interpersonal difficulties (Lucas et al., 2026).

text.text: The changes in social networks we observed post-intervention may therefore reflect some changes in young people's social relationships as they reevaluate their friendships and form connections to new peers.
Nevertheless, it is also important to consider that this may reflect unintended consequences of the trial.
For example, being removed from their typical classes may have reduced participants' time spent with chosen friends, potentially reducing the number of nominations they received.

In the context of the increasing emphasis placed on the prevention of mental health problems in adolescence, including by policymakers (McGorry et al., 2024), and the rising demand for effective interventions for mental health in schools, the findings are potentially clinically important.

text.text: Given its compatibility with existing school mental health support structures, ReSET was designed to be scalable and is well-suited to large-scale replication and pragmatic evaluation.

The trial also demonstrates the feasibility of a whole-school screening-to-intervention pathway: of 4,005 pupils screened, approximately 37% were identified as at-risk, 50% consented to take part and 560 were enrolled, with 90% retained at the 1-year follow-up.

This approach -embedding universal screening within routine school mental health provision rather than relying on help-seeking or referral -has the potential to significantly broaden access, minimise selection bias, and move the field closer to making population-level impacts on mental health problems as demonstrated by our simulations.
However, this simulation is illustrative and relies on a number of assumptions.

Further optimisation of engagement processes would be valuable to increase participation above the 50% achieved in this study and the generalisability of the trial should be considered in context of the population that consented to the study.
A key limitation of this trial is the heterogeneity of facilitators delivering the intervention.
Although all facilitators received standardised training and weekly supervision, professional backgrounds varied across sites, which may have influenced intervention fidelity.
However, we found no statistical evidence of clustering of outcomes by site (Supplementary Materials).
This heterogeneity may also be viewed as a strength, as interventions that do not rely on highly specialised facilitators are more feasible to deliver at scale.

Further limitations are that the study was conducted across 12 sites without an active control condition, meaning that effects could reflect nonspecific factors such as group support or expectancy rather than the intervention itself.
In addition, the outcomes relied on self-report measures of psychopathology rather than clinical diagnoses.

Further evaluation of the intervention at scale with an active control, multiple informants and diagnostic assessments of mental health outcomes would be valuable to assess the potential large-scale effectiveness of the ReSET intervention.

Finally, although we recorded participants' additional service utilisation (e.g., CAMHS or school counselling), this information was provided by school staff at a single point in time, which meant the time since the intervention had ended varied.
Not all schools provided this information, so for both these reasons these data do not reflect a comprehensive record of additional service utilisation by participants.
In conclusion, this cluster-randomised controlled trial evaluated a school-based, indicated preventative intervention targeting transdiagnostic socioemotional processes in adolescence.

The ReSET programme did not produce detectable improvements in overall psychopathology or wellbeing immediately post-intervention but was associated with reductions in overall psychopathology, internalising symptoms, and related transdiagnostic outcomes at 12-month follow-up.
These findings are consistent with a preventative, skillsbased intervention model in which benefits may emerge over time rather than as immediate symptom change.

Taken together to whole-school screening combined with indicated, groupbased transdiagnostic intervention could have the potential to contribute to the prevention of adolescent mental health difficulties in the medium term.
